recipes.title: Any measure as a time series (metric_time + grain)
recipes.when_to_use: Anything "over time": active users per day/week/month (DAU/WAU/MAU), event volume, revenue by day — a count, a count_distinct or a sum on a time axis.
recipes.notes: count_distinct is not additive: a month is re-counted from the fact, never summed from its days — which is why the same measure at two grains is a legitimate question (see same_measure_two_grains). The newest period is partial until the source is fully loaded; check freshness in the semantic_index overview.
recipes.hack: group_by { time: "metric_time", grain } turns ANY measure into a series, and the grain is a QUERY argument — one model answers day, week and month. count counts rows, count_distinct of the entity key counts actors.

recipes.title: Group or filter by an attribute of ANOTHER model
recipes.when_to_use: Any metric sliced or filtered by an attribute that is not on the fact: country, platform, media source, acquisition type, campaign, install date — segmentation of anything.
recipes.notes: The attribute model must OWN the relationship (primary/unique on it); a model with a validity window is joined point-in-time by the layer itself. Filtering works the same way: a where on { model, attribute } filters through the same join.
recipes.hack: Declare use_base_models: ["<model>"] and group_by { model, attribute }: the join runs on the relationship the SCHEMA declares — no key is named at the call site. Any metric x any attribute of any joined model, always this form.

recipes.title: A funnel whose steps are one event + a property value
recipes.when_to_use: A funnel / drop-off over ordered steps recorded as one event with a different payload value (tutorial step_1 → step_2 → step_3) or as different events: onboarding, activation, checkout.
recipes.notes: Every step measure must count the SAME entity, or the ratios are not shares of one population. A step that can be reached twice still counts its user once — that is what count_distinct is for.
recipes.hack: A step = event_name + an event_data value, counted as count_distinct(entity); chain a conversion/ratio metric between consecutive steps. Two steps or six is the same payload. This counts WHO reached each step, not the order they did it in — for the order, and for "within N minutes", use a match_recognize pipeline (pipeline_ordered_sequence).

recipes.title: A conversion metric: B within N days of A
recipes.when_to_use: Any "did they do B within N days of A" question per entity: retention (D1/D7), repeat purchase, trial-to-paid, reactivation, visit-to-purchase conversion.
recipes.notes: The result is a share of the BASE population, not of everyone, and the window is "within", not "exactly on day N" — for the exact offset use pipeline_age_offset_axis. Entities whose window has not elapsed yet drag the rate down: cut the time range to complete windows.
recipes.hack: type: "conversion" + entity + window: "N day" lets the layer pair each base event with a later conversion event PER ENTITY — no self-join, no funnel table. Change N or the event pair for any A→B question; declare two windows to get two horizons in one model.

recipes.title: Two time axes in one query: a cohort axis x the fact's own time
recipes.when_to_use: A cohort grid / retention heatmap: rows = the acquisition (install) cohort, columns = the activity period.
recipes.notes: The cohort axis comes from the dimension model, so it needs use_base_models; the activity axis is the fact's own time. A cell is a metric, so it obeys the same additivity rules — count_distinct per cell cannot be summed along a row.
recipes.hack: Group by a TIME attribute of the joined model (the cohort) and by metric_time (the activity) at once — the grid is just two time dimensions in one group_by. Swap either axis (any cohort attribute, any grain) and the shape holds.

recipes.title: A condition as a measure (sum_boolean)
recipes.when_to_use: Counting rows that satisfy a condition, or splitting the population by "did X" — a behavioural cohort (purchasers vs non-purchasers) without a cohort table.
recipes.notes: sum_boolean counts ROWS, not entities: for "how many users did X" pair it with count_distinct of the entity, or build the flag per entity in a pipeline first. The expression is evaluated on the fact, so a payload column in it needs an event scope.
recipes.hack: agg: "sum_boolean" over a boolean expression counts the rows where it holds, so a flag becomes a measure you can ratio, segment and put on a time axis. Any "did X" population is a boolean measure plus a ratio against the total.

recipes.title: One field, a different aggregation per question
recipes.when_to_use: When the same amount is a total in one question, an average in the next and a p90 in the third: session length, level time, order value, latency, attempts per step.
recipes.notes: An average of an average is wrong: an average measure is computed over the fact rows, so slicing it is safe but combining two of its values is not. A percentile needs the whole distribution — it cannot be derived from other measures.
recipes.hack: The schema MARKS a field aggregatable and fixes no function: each measure picks its own — sum | average | min | max | count | count_distinct | median | percentile (with `percentile`). Declare several measures over ONE field and the model answers "total", "typical" and "tail" at once; group by an ordinal property for a per-step profile.

recipes.title: A ratio metric: one measure divided by another
recipes.when_to_use: Any per-entity or per-row average: ARPU / ARPPU, average order value, revenue per session, events per user, cost per click, a rate per population.
recipes.notes: A ratio is not additive — summing it across slices is meaningless; re-query it at the grain you want. Check the denominator before reading an extreme value: a slice with a tiny population produces a volatile rate, and an empty one has no rate at all.
recipes.hack: type: "ratio" with numerator/denominator METRICS recomputes both sides under every grouping, so the ratio stays correct in every slice: sum ÷ count_distinct = per actor, sum ÷ count = per row. Never divide two numbers you fetched separately.

recipes.title: An event_data property as a measure, its neighbours as dimensions
recipes.when_to_use: An amount recorded in the event payload, broken down by the descriptors on the same event: ad revenue by network / placement / format, purchase value by product, damage by source.
recipes.notes: The unit lives in the schema (e.g. cents): convert it in a derived metric so every consumer divides once, in one place. Grouping by a high-cardinality descriptor (an id) returns a long result — check the value distribution with semantic_index({ source, property }) first.
recipes.hack: A typed payload column is a MEASURE when it is an amount and a DIMENSION when it is a descriptor; scope the model to the event that carries them, then sum the amount and group by its neighbours. The event scope is what makes the payload readable — the same column is NULL on every other event.

recipes.title: The same column under two event scopes, plus a derived net
recipes.when_to_use: A signed two-sided quantity: coins earned vs spent (economy faucets and sinks), credits vs debits, granted vs revoked, gained vs lost — and the net.
recipes.notes: The two measures must cover the same time range and the same population, or the net is a difference of different things. A net near zero can hide two large flows — report both sides next to it.
recipes.hack: Declare the SAME column twice under two event scopes (the in-event and the out-event) and a derived metric subtracts them = net flow. Any two-sided quantity is this shape; the breakdown by category is a group_by on the descriptor both sides carry.

recipes.title: One measure at two grains, divided
recipes.when_to_use: Stickiness (DAU/MAU), repeat rate, frequency — any "share of the longer period's actors that are also in the shorter one".
recipes.notes: The two numbers come from two queries at two grains, and divide the results outside the layer: count_distinct is re-counted per grain, so a month is NOT the sum of its days — which is exactly what makes the ratio meaningful. Keep both raw numbers in the answer; the ratio alone hides whether the base grew or the activity did.
recipes.hack: Query the SAME count_distinct at two grains (day vs month) and divide the results: because count_distinct is re-counted per grain, the two numbers are genuinely different questions. One model, two queries — not two models.

recipes.title: A/B test — conversion rate by variant (with significance)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a conversion rate (e.g. purchase) between experiment variants and test whether the difference is significant.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows are n + conversions per variant (exposed = users with in-window events). Then call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: proportion }): control = the control variant_group row, variants = the rest. For a continuous metric (revenue/ARPU per user), aggregate per-user then per-variant mean+stddev and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }).
recipes.hack: Join the experiments source, window events to [assigned_at, ended_at], flag conversion per user (compute case → aggregate max), then aggregate n + conversions per variant and call experiment({ action: 'analyze' }). Extrapolate: per-variant rate (proportion) or per-user mean+stddev (Welch) for ANY experiment metric.

recipes.title: A cumulative metric: running total, period-to-date, trailing window
recipes.when_to_use: A running total or period-to-date number: cumulative revenue, MTD/WTD, a trailing 7-day sum, an LTV-style accumulation.
recipes.notes: A cumulative metric needs a complete time spine: a day with no rows still exists on the axis, and the metric carries the previous value forward. It is defined at one grain — re-query rather than summing it up to a coarser one.
recipes.hack: type: "cumulative" over a sum measure accumulates along the time spine; grain_to_date resets each period (MTD/WTD); window: "N day" makes it trailing. The spine does the accumulation — never a self-join and never a client-side running sum.

recipes.title: A derived metric: a formula over other metrics
recipes.when_to_use: A composite indicator: blended revenue (IAP + ads), a unit conversion (cents → dollars), ARPDAU from two metrics, a share of one metric in another.
recipes.notes: Only metrics may appear in the expression — a raw column cannot. Each input keeps its own filters and grain, so a derived metric over two differently-scoped measures compares exactly what those scopes say.
recipes.hack: type: "derived" with an `expr` over metric NAMES computes in the layer, so every consumer gets the same formula: unit conversion (x/100), sums of streams, differences, shares. A composite is a formula over metrics, never a new measure over the fact.

recipes.title: A/B test — revenue per user by variant (Welch t-test)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a CONTINUOUS metric (revenue/ARPU/time per user) between experiment variants and test significance.
recipes.hack: Per-user continuous A/B: window events to the assignment period, coalesce the per-event value to 0, sum per user (one value per exposed user), then per variant compute n + avg + stddev and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }) (Welch). Extrapolate to ANY per-user continuous metric (revenue, session time, items) between variants.
recipes.notes: mean A/B needs per-variant n, mean and stddev of a PER-USER value (aggregate per user first, then per variant). experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: mean }) runs Welch t-test: control = control variant_group row, variants = the rest.

recipes.title: A/B test — CUPED variance reduction (pre-experiment covariate)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a continuous metric between variants with MORE POWER by adjusting for each user's pre-experiment value of the same metric (CUPED).
recipes.hack: CUPED = variance reduction via a pre-experiment covariate: per user compute Y (metric inside [assigned_at, ended_at]) and X (same metric BEFORE assigned_at) with two compute-case windows, then per variant emit the sufficient sums n, ΣY, ΣY², ΣX, ΣX², ΣXY (sum of Y, Y*Y, X, X*X, X*Y) and call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: cuped }). Extrapolate: any continuous A/B gains power when a correlated pre-period covariate exists — no per-user data leaves SQL, only the 6 sums.
recipes.notes: CUPED needs a PRE-experiment covariate (the same metric before assignment); it removes its variance, raising power, and reduces to a plain t-test when there is no pre-period signal. Pass per-variant sufficient sums; the tool computes the pooled theta and runs Welch on the adjusted means.

recipes.title: A/B test — ratio metric via the delta method (e.g. level completion rate)
recipes.when_to_use: Compare a RATIO metric between variants where the unit of analysis is finer than the randomization unit — e.g. levels completed per level started, or clicks per impression, when users (not attempts) are randomized.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows carry, per variant: n (users) plus the per-user numerator/denominator sums and their squares/cross-product. Then call experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: ratio }): control = the control variant_group row, variants = the rest. The ratio is Σnumerator/Σdenominator; the delta method turns the per-user sums into a cluster-robust variance, so attempts within a user are not treated as independent.
recipes.hack: For a ratio metric whose denominator is counted at a finer grain than the randomization unit (events/sessions per user), aggregate numerator & denominator PER USER first so each user is one independent observation, then carry forward their squares (num², den²) and cross-product (num·den) and sum per variant. experiment({ action: 'analyze', metric: ratio }) applies the delta method for the correct (cluster-robust) variance — a plain proportion test on pooled events would understate it. Extrapolate to CTR (clicks/impressions), completion rate, ARPDAU, etc.

recipes.title: A/B guardrail — Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) check
recipes.when_to_use: BEFORE trusting any lift: verify the observed per-variant split matches the intended one. A mismatch means randomization or logging is broken and the whole experiment is invalid.
recipes.notes: The native-model pipeline builds a model whose rows are the number of EXPOSED users per variant (distinct users with in-window events). Feed those counts to experiment({ action: 'check_split' }): it runs a χ² goodness-of-fit against the intended split (equal by default; pass expected_ratio for an uneven design). p < 0.001 ⇒ srm_detected=true ⇒ STOP and fix assignment/logging before reading any metric. This is a guardrail, not a metric — run it alongside the metric recipes (conversion/revenue/ratio/cuped).
recipes.hack: Count distinct exposed users per variant in the warehouse, then compare observed vs intended counts with experiment({ action: 'check_split' }) (χ² goodness-of-fit). Extrapolate: ANY 'observed category counts vs an expected split' sanity check (traffic allocation, platform mix, day-of-week balance) is the same χ² test.

recipes.title: A/B planning — sample size & minimum detectable effect (power)
recipes.when_to_use: BEFORE launching, to size the test (how many users per variant to detect a target effect), or given the traffic you have, to find the smallest effect you can detect (MDE). Also AFTER an inconclusive test, to tell 'no effect' apart from 'underpowered'.
recipes.notes: experiment({ action: 'plan' }) is a pure calculation (no warehouse). Provide a baseline rate (metric=proportion) or a stddev (metric=mean) plus EXACTLY ONE of mde (→ required n per group) or n (→ minimum detectable effect). Estimate the baseline/stddev from a monetization_metrics or active_users_trend query first, then plan. Pair every experiment({ action: 'analyze' }) with an up-front MDE so a non-significant result can be read correctly.
recipes.hack: Up-front power analysis: baseline/stddev + target effect → required n per group; or n → MDE. Run it before the test to size it and after an inconclusive test to check it was powered. Extrapolate to any two-arm comparison (proportion z-test or mean t-test).

recipes.title: A table-wide threshold / mean / deviation — one row from an aggregate, never a global window
recipes.when_to_use: You need a number ABOUT the whole table before you can process its rows: a P99 cut-off, a mean and a deviation to standardize by, a max to normalize against.
recipes.approach: Prepare the grain you are asking about (here: revenue per player), then ONE `aggregate` stage with NO group_by: it returns a single row with every statistic you need — the percentile, the mean, the deviation, the max — computed once. Read that row, and use the numbers in the next pass (see agg_scale_rows_by_literals).
recipes.instead_of: The same statistics as analytic windows on every row — `PERCENTILE_CONT(x, 0.99) OVER ()`, `AVG(x) OVER ()`, `STDDEV_POP(x) OVER ()` (a compute `window` stage with no partition_by, or op=raw). A window with no PARTITION BY is ONE window over the whole input: every row is kept and the value is attached to each, so a single worker holds the lot. On a table of millions of rows that is "Resources exceeded during query execution" — and it stays broken after the percentile is removed, because plain AVG/STDDEV over the same global window are just as heavy.
recipes.notes: Say which kind of number you are reporting: on BigQuery `percentile`/`median` here are APPROX_QUANTILES — a sketch, which is exactly why they need no ordering and no global memory; on Postgres they are exact (percentile_cont). The stage description states this per warehouse. An exact percentile over a huge table is the one form that needs a total order, so it is the most expensive thing you can ask for — take the approximate one unless the difference changes a decision, and label it.
recipes.hack: Two passes instead of one query: pass 1 collapses the table to ONE row of statistics (no group_by, no window, no ordering), pass 2 uses those numbers as literals on the rows. Anything you were tempted to write as OVER () belongs in pass 1; a window is only for a value within a group — per player, per day, per session — and then partition_by names that group.

recipes.title: Winsorize and standardize rows by numbers you already computed — plain arithmetic, no window
recipes.when_to_use: Pass 2 after agg_table_stat_no_global_window: clamp outliers at a threshold and turn an amount into a z-score before clustering / scoring.
recipes.approach: Put the numbers from pass 1 in as LITERALS: `least` with parts [{ column }, { value: <p99> }] clamps at the threshold, then `sub` and `div` against { value: <mean> } / { value: <deviation> } give the z-score. Every row is then independent arithmetic — no window, no ordering, no global memory — and the result is the feature table a python stage (or a segmentation) reads.
recipes.instead_of: Recomputing the same statistics per row with AVG/STDDEV/PERCENTILE_CONT OVER () — the global window that exhausts the query's memory. Also: a `sample` stage to make the window affordable, which changes the answer instead of the shape of the query.
recipes.notes: The literals belong to the window of data pass 1 measured — re-run pass 1 when the period or the filter changes, or the z-scores quietly describe a different population. Keep them in the model's description (build_native_model's `description`) so the next reader knows where the numbers came from. div guards against a zero deviation by itself (a NULL, not a division error).
recipes.hack: A number about the whole table enters the row-level query as a constant. Pass 1 (one row of statistics) → pass 2 (arithmetic per row with those constants): the pair replaces every OVER () that had no PARTITION BY, and each pass stays a plain dbt model.

recipes.title: An age axis: join an anchor date, then date_diff
recipes.when_to_use: Anything measured in "days since": exact day-N retention, a lifetime / LTV curve, age buckets, time-to-first-purchase.
recipes.notes: The offset is exact ("on day N"), which is a different question from a conversion window ("within N days"). Offsets whose day has not arrived yet are missing rather than zero — cut the range to complete offsets before reading a curve.
recipes.hack: Join the per-entity anchor date, date_diff it against the event time, group by the offset: that offset column is the axis a lifetime curve, an exact day-N series and a cohort heatmap all share. Change the unit for hours or weeks.

recipes.title: Episodes from a gap: lag → gap → flag → running sum
recipes.when_to_use: Sessionization and any episode grouping when no id for it is recorded: sessions from raw events by an inactivity gap, visits, streaks, playtime bouts.
recipes.notes: The first row of each entity has a NULL previous timestamp and must count as a new episode, or every entity loses its first one. The running sum requires an order — the window's order_by is part of the definition, not decoration.
recipes.hack: Four stages: window lag (previous timestamp per entity) → date_diff (the gap) → compute case (does this row start a new episode?) → window sum (running episode index). Aggregating by (entity, index) yields one row per episode with its depth and duration. The threshold is the only thing that changes between products.

recipes.title: Compare a row to the previous one: aggregate, then lag
recipes.when_to_use: DoD / WoW / MoM readouts: a metric per period plus its change versus the previous period, growth rates, "versus the previous row" comparisons.
recipes.notes: The first period has no previous value: its delta is NULL, not zero. Division by a previous zero yields NULL — guard it with nullif if the result feeds a chart.
recipes.hack: Aggregate to the grain FIRST, then window lag over the ordered result and subtract/divide. The lag must run over the AGGREGATED rows — over raw events it compares two events, not two periods. Swap the grain or the offset freely.

recipes.title: Data or behaviour: volume and NULL coverage before the metric
recipes.when_to_use: FIRST move when a number looks wrong or moved: did the events change volume (tracking broke, a release dropped an event) or did behaviour change? Also a smoke test of a new event.
recipes.notes: Distinguish an EXPECTED NULL (the property does not belong to that event) from a gap (it does and is missing) — the property view reports them separately. A volume change with stable coverage is behaviour; stable volume with collapsing coverage is instrumentation.
recipes.hack: Count rows and distinct actors per event, then read the properties' NULL coverage (semantic_index({ source, property })) before trusting any movement. Triage order: volume → coverage → metric; most "metric drops" are a tracking change, and this ordering is what tells the two apart.

recipes.title: Two-sample significance for ANY two groups (no experiment needed)
recipes.when_to_use: You have TWO groups from the SAME pipeline and want to know if a difference is statistically real — NOT a randomized experiment. E.g. mean time-to-first vs time-to-last occurrence, conversion of cohort A vs B, a metric before vs after a date, organic vs paid. There is NO experiments-assignment table involved.
recipes.notes: Don't hand-roll a t-test/z-test. Compute per-group aggregates with a build_native_model pipeline, then feed them to ab_test — 'control'/'variants' are just group A vs group B(…). For a CONTINUOUS metric (time, value, count per unit): aggregate per group to n + mean (avg) + stddev, then ab_test({ metric: 'mean' }) (Welch t-test). For a RATE: aggregate to conversions + n per group, then ab_test({ metric: 'proportion' }) (two-proportion z-test). The pipeline that produces the groups can be ANY grouping — a CASE/derive column, two event_data values, a date split — it does NOT require the experiments role. The tool_calls below show the final ab_test step on example per-group aggregates.
recipes.hack: Compare two groups → aggregate each to its sufficient stats (mean: n+mean+stddev; proportion: conversions+n) in one pipeline, then ONE ab_test call returns lift + p-value + CI + significance. Reuse for first-vs-last, before-vs-after, cohort-vs-cohort — anywhere you'd otherwise eyeball two numbers.

recipes.title: A value from a lookup — merge, never map
recipes.when_to_use: You have a mapping (id → label, day → target, country → tier) and want it as a column.
recipes.approach: Put the other side in a frame and MERGE on the key: `lookup = bpd.DataFrame({"k": [...], "v": [...]}); df = df.merge(lookup, on="k", how="left")`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["v"] = df["k"].map(mapping)` — map aligns two objects by index, and the frame from dbt.ref() has none: NullIndexError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: The dict keys must have the SAME type as the column they join on — bpd.DataFrame turns Python strings into STRING, so a numeric key needs numbers, not "1". how="left" keeps unmatched rows with NULL; how="inner" drops them, which is a different question. If a merge is awkward (a big mapping, a key that needs normalising), the alternatives in order are: build the lookup as a SQL stage BEFORE the python one and let the pipeline join it, or set_index on both sides around the operation. `df.join(other, on=…)` is NOT the same as merge: join goes through the align path and needs an index.
recipes.hack: Any "value from somewhere else" is a merge: a dict, a groupby result, a second table, a threshold per group. Build the other side as a frame with the key as a COLUMN, then merge.

recipes.title: A group's aggregate back on its rows — transform or merge
recipes.when_to_use: Share of a group's total, deviation from a group mean, "how big is my cohort" as a column.
recipes.approach: Same number of rows → `df["m"] = df.groupby("k")["x"].transform("mean")` (broadcasts inside ONE frame). A different shape, or several aggregates → build it with `groupby(..., as_index=False)` and MERGE it back.
recipes.instead_of: `df["m"] = df.groupby("k")["x"].mean()` — the groupby result is another object with its own index; assigning it needs alignment the frame cannot do.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: as_index=False keeps the key as a COLUMN — without it the key becomes the index and there is nothing to merge on. rename() before the merge, or both sides bring a column of the same name and the merge suffixes them.
recipes.hack: Two forms, one rule: inside one frame — transform; between two frames — merge. Never assignment.

recipes.title: Distinct values — a groupby, not unique()
recipes.when_to_use: A distinct list of ids, of (user, level) pairs, of values a column takes.
recipes.approach: De-duplicate in place: `uniq = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["k"])[["k"]]` — or, for one column, `df["k"].unique(keep_order=False)`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["k"].unique()` with no argument — its default keep_order=True demands a row ordering and raises OrderRequiredError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: drop_duplicates needs no ordering: it compiles to a ROW_NUMBER over a partition by the key, so which duplicate survives is arbitrary — for a distinct LIST that is exactly right, and for "keep the newest row per key" it is not (sort first, or aggregate). unique(keep_order=False) is the aggregate form (ANY_VALUE per key). A groupby on the key is the third form and the one to use when the counts are wanted too.
recipes.hack: De-duplication is a GROUPING, not a row operation: name the columns that define uniqueness and keep one row per group. Nothing here needs the row order unless you want to choose WHICH row survives.

recipes.title: Top-N and anything positional — sort_values first
recipes.when_to_use: Top/bottom N, "the largest", "the first row per group", anything positional.
recipes.approach: Say what "first" means, then take rows: `top = df.sort_values("x", ascending=False).head(10)`.
recipes.instead_of: `df.head(10)` / `df.tail(10)` / `df.iloc[:10]` on an unsorted frame, and `df.nlargest(10, "x")` — every one of them raises OrderRequiredError here (nlargest only escapes it with keep="all", because ties then need no tie-break).
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: This frame has no row order of its own, so "the first N" is undefined until a sort defines it — and the library refuses rather than returning an arbitrary slice: head, tail, iat, sample, rank, melt, unstack, reset_index and every cum*/shift/diff/rolling are marked as needing an ordering. sort_values is what grants it (the sorted node reports itself as explicitly ordered), and it grants it to everything after. For a quick LOOK at data use peek(n) — it needs no ordering, but it returns pandas, so it is for inspection only, never the stage result.
recipes.hack: Order is data: state it with sort_values wherever the answer depends on position, and never rely on the order rows happen to arrive in. One sort is enough for the whole function.

recipes.title: Rolling / shift / cumulative — sort, then the operation
recipes.when_to_use: 7-day averages, day-over-day deltas, cumulative totals, previous-value comparisons.
recipes.approach: `df = df.sort_values(order_key)` and then the series operation: `rolling(window=n).mean()`, `shift(1)`, `cumsum()`, `diff()`, `pct_change()`.
recipes.instead_of: Calling rolling/shift/cumsum on the frame as it arrives — the window is then over an arbitrary order, and the numbers are silently meaningless.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: Aggregate to the grain of the series FIRST (one row per day here) — rolling over raw events is both wrong and expensive. The first window-1 rows come back NULL by definition: say so, or drop them in a following SQL stage.
recipes.hack: Order-dependent operations are a pair: sort_values on the axis, then the operation. One sort is enough for the whole function.

recipes.title: A statistic OF the frame back ON it — a broadcast scalar
recipes.when_to_use: z-score, share of total, distance from the mean, normalisation.
recipes.approach: An aggregate OF the frame applied back TO it: `df["z"] = (df["x"] - df["x"].mean()) / df["x"].std()`; `df["share"] = df["x"] / df["x"].sum()`.
recipes.instead_of: Computing the statistic in another frame and joining it in (it is a different root, so it needs a merge), and `std(ddof=…)` — this Series.std takes NO parameters at all, so passing ddof is a TypeError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: mean()/sum()/std()/min()/max()/count() of the SAME frame come back as real scalars and broadcast over its rows — one statement, no alignment. std() here is the SAMPLE deviation (N-1) and has no ddof: if you need the population form, write it out — ((s - s.mean()) ** 2).mean() ** 0.5 — and say which one the number is. quantile(q) with a single q is a scalar too; with a list it becomes an indexed Series, which this frame cannot align.
recipes.hack: Whole-frame statistic → scalar → column. Safe for mean, sum, std, var, min, max, count and a single quantile; anything that returns a SERIES (several quantiles, a groupby aggregate) has to be merged back instead.

recipes.title: A threshold from the distribution — one quantile as a scalar
recipes.when_to_use: "The slowest 10%", "unusually hard levels", any "above normal" where nobody has defined normal.
recipes.approach: `cut = df["x"].quantile(0.9)` (a SCALAR) → write it as a column and compare: `df["p90"] = cut; df["is_high"] = df["x"] >= cut`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["x"].quantile([0.5, 0.9])` — a SERIES indexed by q, which this runtime has no index to align; and a hard-coded threshold nobody can defend.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: Ask for ONE q at a time. Several quantiles at once belong in a SQL stage (aggregate with fn=percentile), which returns them as columns instead of an indexed series. Keeping the threshold as a column makes the cut visible in the result instead of hidden in a filter.
recipes.hack: A cut-off computed FROM the data (median, p90, IQR) written back as a column, then compared row by row.

recipes.title: Filtering by another frame's data — merge the flag in
recipes.when_to_use: Keeping only qualifying users, excluding a blacklist, filtering by a per-group condition.
recipes.approach: Merge the other side in and filter on the merged column: `df = df.merge(flags, on="k", how="inner")` (or how="left" then `df[df["flag"]]`).
recipes.instead_of: `df[other["flag"]]` / `df[df["k"].isin(other_series)]` — a Series from ANOTHER frame has no index to align with this one.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: A mask built from the SAME frame (df[df["x"] > 0], and any & / | of such masks) is always fine — this rule is only about a condition that lives in another object. An inner merge on the key IS the semi-join SQL would run; dropping the helper column keeps the output clean. Watch the root: a mask taken before a cache() or from an estimator's output belongs to a different expression, and using it here raises.
recipes.hack: "Keep the rows that are in X" = build X as a frame of keys and inner-merge it. Same move for "exclude": merge with how="left" and keep the NULLs.

recipes.title: A prediction per row — return the estimator's frame, do not assign its column
recipes.when_to_use: Clustering, scoring, classification, a predicted value per row.
recipes.approach: Fit inside BigQuery, then RETURN what predict gives you: `model.fit(scaled); out = model.predict(df); return out` — that frame already holds every input column plus the prediction (CENTROID_ID for clustering, predicted_<label> for a supervised model). Declare those columns in `output.columns`.
recipes.instead_of: `df["segment"] = model.predict(X)["CENTROID_ID"]` — predict re-reads its result as a NEW query, so its frame has a different root than df and the assignment raises NullIndexError. Also sklearn/scipy: they need to_pandas() first and then run single-node.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: predict/transform/fit_transform all go through the same path: the input is wrapped in a BigQuery ML table function whose output "includes all input columns, with new columns appended", and the result is read back as its own query. So the prediction never has to be carried over — return the output frame and let the SQL stages after it do the grouping. Scale first when the algorithm is distance-based; the scaler returns its own frame the same way, so feed it to fit rather than assigning it back.
recipes.hack: Feature table in SQL → fit/predict in one python stage → the estimator's OWN frame out → profile it in SQL. The shape holds for every estimator; only the class and the appended column change.

recipes.title: An estimator's parameters are BQML's, not scikit-learn's — and scaling is a step, not a flag
recipes.when_to_use: Before passing any parameter to a bigframes.ml estimator, and whenever features must be standardized for a distance-based model (KMeans, PCA).
recipes.approach: Pass only the parameters the signature has, and let a TRANSFORMER do the scaling: `Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", KMeans(n_clusters=4))])`, fit it, return what predict gives back. KMeans is (n_clusters, *, init, init_col, distance_type, max_iter, tol, warm_start) — everything after the `*` is keyword-only; StandardScaler() takes no parameters at all; Pipeline takes EXACTLY TWO steps, (transform, estimator).
recipes.instead_of: `KMeans(n_clusters=4, standardize_features=True)` → TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument. bigframes.ml wears the scikit-learn API but wraps BigQuery ML: a constructor takes the options its BQML model type has, so an sklearn-only argument (standardize_features, n_init, random_state, algorithm) does not exist here. A third Pipeline step raises NotImplementedError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) for the signature of the class you are about to build (every bigframes.ml constructor, extracted from the installed library), and semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) for the frame rules this recipe rests on.
recipes.notes: Why the resemblance misleads: each estimator maps its parameters to BQML CREATE MODEL options (cluster.py _BQML_PARAMS_MAPPING / _bqml_options), so the surface is BQML's and nothing else is accepted — and the parameters after the first are keyword-only, so a positional call fails the same way. The signatures are extracted from the installed library (config/bigframes-facts.json) and published as a fetchable reference — semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) — so they are this version's, not a memory of the docs. Standardizing in a SQL stage before the python stage is equally valid and cheaper — compute the mean and the deviation as a ONE-ROW aggregate and apply them as literals (see agg_table_stat_no_global_window); then the estimator needs no transformer at all.
recipes.hack: Read the signature, pass only what is in it, and express anything it lacks as a step of its own (a transformer) or as SQL before the stage. The same holds for every estimator: only the class and its option names change.

recipes.title: An estimator whose output REPLACES the frame — declare its columns
recipes.when_to_use: Forecasting, model metrics, a transformed matrix — anything where the result is not "my rows plus a column".
recipes.approach: When the estimator returns its OWN shape (forecast, score, metrics), the python stage returns THAT frame and `output.columns` describes it: `out = model.predict(horizon=30); return out`.
recipes.instead_of: Declaring the input columns as the output — the following SQL stages then reference columns that do not exist.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: The declared columns above are what ARIMA_PLUS.FORECAST produces; verify them on the first run (the result reports its columns) and rename in a following SQL stage if you want your own names. This is the same rule as the prediction recipe seen from the other side: an estimator hands back a frame of its own, and the stage returns THAT — the difference is only whether its shape is your rows (predict) or something else entirely (a forecast, a score, metrics). History IS the input: one row per period, no gaps. One model per series — a per-segment forecast is one model per segment, not one call.
recipes.hack: Whenever an estimator's output is its own table (forecast, score, metrics, transform), the stage's output.columns describes THAT table — and the SQL after it works on those names.

recipes.title: A supervised model — fit(X, y) with a LABEL, and the predicted_<label> column it returns
recipes.when_to_use: Predicting a number (spend, days to churn) or a class (will pay, will churn) per row: regression and classification.
recipes.approach: Label and features are SEPARATE arguments: `model.fit(df[features], df[[label]])` — the label is a FRAME (double brackets), not a Series. Predict on the features only (`model.predict(df.drop(columns=[label]))`) and return that frame: it carries every column you passed plus `predicted_<label>` (and, for a classifier, `predicted_<label>_probs`, an array of {label, prob}). Declare those names in `output.columns` and profile them in a SQL stage after.
recipes.instead_of: `model.fit(df)` with the label still inside the features (it then predicts itself), a Series as y, or assigning `df["pred"] = model.predict(...)` — predict re-reads its result, so the assignment raises NullIndexError. Also sklearn's LogisticRegression/RandomForest: they need to_pandas() and run single-node.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) for the estimator's own parameters, and semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) for the frame rules this recipe rests on.
recipes.notes: The label column must be OUT of the features, or the model learns the answer from itself. A classifier's `predicted_<label>_probs` is an ARRAY of structs — pass it through or unnest it, do not aggregate it as a number. Training here is a BQML CREATE MODEL: it is charged as a query and the model lives in the dataset for the session. How good the model is is a separate question — see bf_ml_evaluate_with_split; a prediction without an evaluation is a number with no error bar.
recipes.hack: Prepare ONE table in SQL where the label is a column next to the features, then fit(features, label) and return the prediction frame. The same shape covers every supervised estimator — LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, XGB*, RandomForest* — only the class and the predicted column's name change.

recipes.title: How good is the model — train_test_split, then score() as a one-row metrics table
recipes.when_to_use: Before reporting any prediction: an honest error/accuracy figure, measured on rows the model did not train on.
recipes.approach: Split inside BigQuery — `X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)` — fit on the train half and return `model.score(X_test, y_test)`: ONE row of metrics, which is the stage's whole output. Regression gives mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, mean_squared_log_error, median_absolute_error, r2_score, explained_variance; classification gives precision, recall, accuracy, f1_score, log_loss, roc_auc. Declare exactly those in `output.columns`.
recipes.instead_of: Scoring on the training rows (an accuracy that means nothing), splitting with a pandas train_test_split after to_pandas(), or reporting a prediction with no error figure at all.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) for train_test_split's own parameters (test_size, train_size, random_state, stratify, shuffle), and semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) for the frame rules.

functions.name: evaluate
body: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=test_size)

recipes.notes: The metric names are the model type's, so declare the set that matches yours (the six above are the classifier's; a regressor returns the error/r2 set). score() returns ONE row — this is the output-replaces-the-frame case, so nothing downstream should expect the input columns. KFold and cross_validate live in the same module when one split is not enough. A split is random: pass random_state for a repeatable number, and stratify for a rare class.
recipes.hack: Split, fit on one half, score on the other, return the metrics frame. It is the same three lines for every estimator — and it is what turns a prediction into a result you can report.

recipes.title: Many correlated features into a few — PCA, whose output REPLACES the frame
recipes.when_to_use: A feature table with many overlapping columns before clustering or a model: compress it to a few components, or find how much of the variance the first ones carry.
recipes.approach: `pca = PCA(n_components=2); pca.fit(df[features]); out = pca.predict(df[features]); return out` — the result is `principal_component_1 … principal_component_N`, NOT your rows with columns added, so `output.columns` names exactly those. `pca.explained_variance_ratio_` is a frame of its own (principal_component_id, explained_variance_ratio) — return THAT instead when the question is how much variance the components carry.
recipes.instead_of: Expecting the input columns back (the SQL stages after it would then reference columns that do not exist), or assigning a component into df (a cross-frame assignment → NullIndexError). Also sklearn's PCA: it needs to_pandas() and runs single-node.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) for PCA's parameters (n_components, svd_solver), and semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) for the frame rules.
recipes.notes: Scale first when the features live on different scales (StandardScaler as the first of Pipeline's two steps, or the mean/deviation applied in SQL — see agg_scale_rows_by_literals): PCA follows variance, so an unscaled large column dominates the components. Whether a column you passed but did not train on (a player id) comes back alongside the components is BQML's pass-through behaviour — verify it on the first run (the result reports its columns) rather than assuming it. Components are not features with meaning: name them by what they correlate with before reporting anything about them.
recipes.hack: Fit on the feature matrix, return what predict gives back, and declare ITS columns. Anything whose output is its own table — PCA, a forecast, score(), a transformer — is declared the same way.

recipes.title: Categorical features into a model — a ColumnTransformer as the first of Pipeline's two steps
recipes.when_to_use: Features that are not numbers (country, platform, media source, an event name) alongside numeric ones in one model.
recipes.approach: Put the encoding in the model, not in your code: `ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), [<numeric columns>]), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(), [<categorical columns>])])` as step one, the estimator as step two, and `Pipeline` over exactly those two. Fit the pipeline on the prepared table and return `pipe.predict(...)` — the encoded columns stay inside the model and never reach your output.
recipes.instead_of: Hand-rolled dummies with np.where / a lookup frame per value (a cross-frame alignment → NullIndexError, and a column per value you have to keep in step), a THIRD Pipeline step (NotImplementedError — it takes exactly two), or LabelEncoder on a nominal column, which invents an order between its values.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ recipe: "bf_ml_signatures" }) for the transformers' parameters (OneHotEncoder(drop, min_frequency, max_categories), KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins, strategy), and the scalers, which take none), and semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) for the frame rules.

functions.name: classify_with_categoricals
body: prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), numeric), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(), categorical)])

recipes.notes: Pipeline accepts ONE transform step and ONE estimator; a ColumnTransformer is how several transformers fit into that one slot. Its entries are (name, transformer, columns) and the transformers allowed inside it are the preprocessing/impute ones plus SQLScalarColumnTransformer, which carries a scalar SQL expression when nothing else fits. A high-cardinality column (a campaign id, a device model) is a column per value inside the model — cut it down first (min_frequency / max_categories on OneHotEncoder, or a CASE in a SQL stage that keeps the top values and folds the rest into 'other').
recipes.hack: Encoding belongs to the model, so it is applied identically at training and at prediction. Numeric columns through a scaler, categorical through OneHotEncoder, both inside one ColumnTransformer, that transformer plus the estimator inside Pipeline — and the stage returns the prediction frame.

recipes.title: An expensive intermediate read twice — cache()
recipes.when_to_use: One heavy join or aggregate feeding several outputs in the same function.
recipes.approach: Materialize it once, then derive everything from the cached object: `joined = df.merge(other, on="k"); joined.cache()` — and only after that build the results that read it.
recipes.instead_of: Deriving several results from the same expensive expression without caching (deferred execution re-runs it per dependent result), and mixing objects taken BEFORE the cache with the cached frame — cache() swaps the object's node for a read of the temporary table, so a mask or column taken earlier belongs to the old expression and combining them raises NullIndexError.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: cache() writes a temporary BigQuery table you pay to store, so use it for an intermediate that is genuinely read more than once (a join, a heavy groupby), not for every line. It returns self and replaces the node in place — which is why the order matters: cache first, derive after.
recipes.hack: Deferred execution means "written once" is not "computed once". If two or more results read the same intermediate, cache it — and take everything downstream from the object you cached.

recipes.title: What only SQL can do — bigframes.bigquery (bbq)
recipes.when_to_use: LEAST/GREATEST, array aggregation, building a STRUCT column, epoch conversions, a SQL function with no pandas name.
recipes.approach: Reach the BigQuery function directly: `bbq.sql_scalar("LEAST({0}, {1})", columns=[df["a"], df["b"]])`, `bbq.array_agg(df.groupby("k")["c"])`, `bbq.struct(df[["a","b"]])`, `bbq.unix_micros(df["t"])`.
recipes.instead_of: `to_pandas()` to get a Python equivalent — that leaves BigQuery and brings the whole result into the notebook.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: sql_scalar takes a single-column expression with {0}, {1} … placeholders bound to the columns you pass — it is not a place for a whole query. Everything in bbq still compiles to SQL and runs in BigQuery.
recipes.hack: Before converting to pandas for a missing function, look in bbq: arrays, structs, epochs and an arbitrary scalar SQL expression are all there.

recipes.title: Leaving for pandas only after the aggregation
recipes.when_to_use: A library call that only exists in pandas/numpy, on a small aggregated result.
recipes.approach: Aggregate in the warehouse FIRST, convert the small result: `small = df.groupby("k", as_index=False)["x"].sum(); pdf = small.to_pandas()`.
recipes.instead_of: `pdf = df.to_pandas()` on the incoming frame — it downloads the whole table into the notebook runtime and everything after it is single-node.
recipes.read_first: semantic_index({ guide: "python" }) first — the frame rules of this runtime. This recipe is ONE approach from it, filled in and compiling.
recipes.notes: The model must return a frame this runtime can materialize, so a pandas result goes back with bpd.read_pandas(). Do this only when the operation genuinely has no frame equivalent — and only on an already-aggregated table, because the download and everything after it happen on one node.
recipes.hack: The boundary is a decision, not a convenience: aggregate, then convert, then convert back. If the frame you hand to to_pandas() could be large, the approach is wrong.

recipes.title: A non-events source: the same amount under several aggregations
recipes.when_to_use: A fact whose columns are amounts rather than events (spend, inventory, balances) — and a question that needs the total, the peak and the tail of one of them.
recipes.notes: The measures above read the SAME column at sum, max, average and p90 — nothing in the schema decided that. Such a source has its own time axis, so metric_time means its dates, not an events fact's; joining it to per-event data is many-to-many by design (carry its attributes onto events, never sum its money over them).
recipes.hack: The schema marks a column aggregatable and fixes NO function: every measure names the field and picks its own agg, so one model answers "total", "peak", "typical" and "tail" at once. Extrapolate: any amount, any of sum | average | min | max | median | percentile | count | count_distinct, chosen per question.

recipes.title: A measure the SCHEMA governs: name it, never redeclare it
recipes.when_to_use: When a number has to be identical across tasks and people — the schema already publishes it with its function fixed.
recipes.notes: The task declares no `measures` block at all: it names the governed measure and adds only the attributes it wants to slice by. The free choice over the raw field stays available in a separate model (measures_source_agg_choice) — the governed twin exists so two tasks cannot disagree about "the total".
recipes.hack: A schema entry that carries `agg` publishes a measure whose function is fixed for everyone; a task consumes it by NAME. Use it when comparability matters, and the per-question agg when the function is part of the question. The semantic_index model view lists which measures are governed.

recipes.title: Two independent sources answering one query (never mixed)
recipes.when_to_use: A question that spans two facts — activity and crashes, activity and spend — where each side has its own vocabulary.
recipes.notes: Each semantic model names its own `from` and is scoped with its own event vocabulary — an event or property of one source is not readable on the other, and there is no default source. What makes them comparable is metric_time: both are put on the same axis without being joined.
recipes.hack: One context, several `semantic_models`, each with its own `from`: the layer answers both in one query and lines them up over metric_time. Extrapolate: any number of sources side by side; a RATIO across two of them belongs in a derived metric, not in a measure.

recipes.title: A pipeline join by the relationship name (and its variants)
recipes.when_to_use: Matching two facts on a key nobody owns — the same funnel id, the same order id, the same session — which the governed path cannot join.
recipes.notes: The join names `via: "<relationship>"` and nothing else — the key columns (here a funnel id PLUS the entity, two columns) come from the schema, and the two sides may spell them differently. Both sides keep their own column names, so take from the other side only what you need (`attrs`) and never a name this side already has. Where a side carries the relationship in several alternative columns, each is offered as `<relationship>_<variant>` and the CALLER picks the one the question is about (the semantic_index model view lists them); an empty variant column matches nothing, and a left join is what keeps the unmatched rows. Joins STACK: another join stage reaches a third source.
recipes.hack: A many-to-many match (several rows share the id on both sides) has no governed path by design — MetricFlow only joins onto a unique key — so it is a pipeline join, declared by relationship name. Extrapolate: any declared relationship, plus `on:` as the ad-hoc fallback when both sides name one column identically.

recipes.title: Joining a slowly-changing model: state the window
recipes.when_to_use: Joining attributes that CHANGE (an install record, a plan, a price list) — anything with a validity window.
recipes.notes: Without `between`, the key alone matches EVERY historical version of the row: the count and any money inflate silently (the add_step response nudges about it and names the real window columns). The value side is the time being asked about — the event time, the spend day, or a funnel's first event after a match_recognize stage. The governed path applies the window itself; a pipeline states it here, deliberately, so the moment is visible at the call site.
recipes.hack: Point-in-time = the key AND a time inside the window: `between: { value: <the time asked about>, from: <validity start>, to: <validity end> }`. The window is half-open on the right — the CURRENT version has no end (NULL) and must still match. Extrapolate: any versioned dimension.

recipes.title: An ORDERED sequence per entity (row-pattern match)
recipes.when_to_use: When the order matters: did A happen before B, how far along an ordered path each entity got, time between steps.
recipes.notes: One row per entity (or per match with rows: "one_per_match"), with a reached flag and a timestamp per step, so the drop-off between steps and the time spent in each are both readable from the same result. A step is an event plus a payload condition — the same definition the metric funnel uses, here with the ORDER enforced. It scans ONE source: a sequence cannot span two facts.
recipes.hack: mode: "ordered" + partition_by the entity + a step list = the row-pattern scan. Count the flags for a funnel that respects order, diff the timestamps for time-between-steps, add `within` for "inside N minutes". Extrapolate: any ordered path (onboarding, checkout, an ad funnel, a support escalation).

recipes.title: One row per element of an array payload (unnest)
recipes.when_to_use: A property that holds a LIST (items collected, tags, stack frames, breadcrumbs) and a question about the elements.
recipes.notes: unnest MULTIPLIES rows (one per element), so count after it counts elements, not source rows — keep a count_distinct of the source key next to it to stay honest. An array of structs is unnested the same way with `field:` to pick one member, or without it and then a compute json_field per member. The array encoding (a native array vs a JSON-encoded string) is declared in the schema, not at the call site.
recipes.hack: unnest turns a list into rows, after which every ordinary stage applies (group, filter, join). Extrapolate: element frequency, co-occurrence (unnest twice), "reports containing X" (unnest then filter then count_distinct of the source key).

recipes.title: Reshape the result: columns into rows (and back)
recipes.when_to_use: When the shape is wrong for what reads it: several measure columns that should be (name, value) rows, or categories that should be columns.
recipes.notes: unpivot folds the named columns into (metric, value) rows — the long form a chart or a per-metric comparison wants; `pivot` does the reverse (group_by + on + fn + value_column + the values to spread), which returns ONE row per group and as many columns as values. Both are the LAST shaping step: aggregate first, reshape after.
recipes.hack: Shape is a stage, not a rewrite: unpivot to compare metrics as rows, pivot to lay a category out as columns. Extrapolate: any wide result to long for a chart, any long result to wide for a table.
